C0.quote: pairwise comparisons capture the majority relation between pairs of candidates
C0.note: Tournament solutions are aggregation rules on the majority relation, with elections given as an application. Eligibility is borderline because sports tournaments are also an application.

C1.quote: using axiomatic and probabilistic analysis (Section 3) as well as through experiments
C1.note: Includes a probabilistic result (Theorem 15) on uniform random tournaments, coded under AX/SI.

C2.1.quote: A tournament solution is a function that maps each tournament

C2.2.quote: represents an asymmetric and connex dominance relation between the alternatives

C2.3.quote: We used six stochastic models to generate preferences
C2.3.note: Preferences are referred to only in the experimental generation of tournaments (some models with voters).

C2.4.quote: pairwise comparisons capture the majority relation between pairs of candidates
C2.4.note: The tournament is treated as the majority relation derived from preferences, with no statement about submission or reporting.

C3.1.quote: a natural interpretation in terms of bribery and manipulation
C3.1.note: Bribery and manipulation appear only as an interpretation of MoV; no strategic analysis is carried out.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost or distortion notion is used for voters.

C5.1.quote: inherits Pareto optimality from the uncovered set, which it refines
C5.1.note: Pareto is mentioned only in passing in Section 3.1 and in the Discussion, not in any result.

VOT.note: No voter takes an action in the formal model; tournaments are given or randomly generated.

BRI.note: Bribery appears only as an interpretation of MoV, not as a modelled agent.
